sections.summary: Paul instructs the community on Spirit-led responses to a member's transgression, mutual burden-bearing, honest self-examination, and individual responsibility before God.
Paul gives practical instruction that those who receive oral teaching should share material goods with those who teach them.

sections.section_title: Sowing and Reaping — The Flesh-Spirit Contrast Applied
sections.summary: Paul applies the sowing-reaping principle to the flesh-Spirit contrast, declaring that the one who sows to the flesh reaps corruption and the one who sows to the Spirit reaps eternal life.
sections.relevance: The passage directly presents salvation outcomes — eternal life versus corruption — as determined by human choice. The reflexive 'his own flesh' emphasizes that sowing is a personal decision, and the universal law 'whatever one sows, that will he also reap' frames the harvest as corresponding to the human agent's investment. The conditional 'if we do not give up' makes perseverance a genuine factor in the outcome. The entire framework treats human agency as determinative: the person chooses the field (flesh or Spirit), and the harvest follows accordingly.
key_phrases: whatever one sows, that will he also reap
the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption
the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life
if we do not give up

sections.section_title: Paul's Handwritten Conclusion — The Cross Against Circumcision
sections.summary: Paul exposes the agitators' motives of vanity and cowardice, declares the cross as the sole basis for boasting, proclaims new creation as the only category that matters, and pronounces blessing on those who walk by this standard as the Israel of God.
sections.relevance: The blessing in verse 16 is conditioned on those who 'walk by this rule' — the verb stoicheo implies ongoing human choice to align with the standard of new creation. Belonging to the 'Israel of God' is tied to walking by the cross-centered rule, not to a prior divine determination. The passage frames standing before God as connected to a human posture (walking by the rule of new creation) rather than to an irrevocable divine decree, though its primary focus is the cross-circumcision contrast rather than the determinism question directly.
key_phrases: as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them
neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation
